title.en: Command Line, Git and Reproducible Environments
title.ar: سطر الأوامر وGit والبيئات القابلة لإعادة الإنتاج

tagline: Set up work that another person can rebuild from a clean machine: shell scripts, a reviewed Git history, locked environments, a container and no secrets in history
description: Participants set up work that another person can rebuild from a clean machine. They script the shell, use Git with branches, pull requests and review on a shared repository, resolve a merge conflict, lock dependencies, run a project in a container without administrator rights, and keep secrets out of history.
audience: Beginners. Graduates and career changers heading for analysis, data science, data engineering or AI engineering courses, and computing graduates whose degree did not require testing, version control or reproducible environments.
prerequisites: Writes and runs a short program in Python or another language

outcomes.text: Explain how Git records history as commits, branches and remotes, and what each everyday command changes, given diagrams of a repository and sequences of commands
outcomes.evidence: commit graphs drawn correctly for four of five sequences in a supervised check

outcomes.text: Use the shell to inspect and transform files, combining commands with pipes and a short script, given a folder of synthetic log and comma-separated files
outcomes.evidence: a script that produces the requested counts and runs unchanged on a second folder

outcomes.text: Apply a branch, pull request and review workflow, including resolving a merge conflict, given a team repository with a protected main branch
outcomes.evidence: a merged pull request with review comments addressed and a resolved conflict in the history

outcomes.text: Configure an isolated environment with locked dependencies and run the project in a container without administrator rights, given an analysis project that fails on a second machine
outcomes.evidence: a lock file, a container definition and a clean rebuild that reproduces the expected output

outcomes.text: Prepare a repository that keeps secrets out of history, and carry out the response when one leaks, given a project needing an API key, with a seeded leaked key in an old commit
outcomes.evidence: configuration read from the environment, a passing secret scan and a rotation note

outcomes.text: Deliver a repository that a peer reproduces on a clean machine using only its README, given the participant's own small project
outcomes.evidence: the peer's reproduction log and fixes for every step the peer could not follow

case_study.name: The air-quality monitoring company
case_study.summary: A private contractor (fictional, unnamed) that runs twelve dust and particle sensor stations, ST01 to ST12, at four clients' sites in one unnamed city; its monthly client report is a Python project that only runs on the analyst's laptop. Every lab works on synthetic hourly logs for October and November 2026 generated with a fixed seed, with planted traps (comment lines, Windows line endings, duplicate lines after a logger restart, a two-day gap), and on a seeded report-portal key whose prefix is the course's own; people appear only as roles.

format_note: Intensive: 3 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task

days.title: The shell and the commit graph

sessions.title: Paths and permissions
sessions.summary: Where you are, how a path is read, and who may read, change or run a file
outcomes: Tell an absolute path from a relative one and predict where each points after a move
Read a permission string and say who may read, write or run the file
Make a script independent of the folder it is run from

lab.title: Find your way round the project folder
lab.summary: Addition to the entry's labs. Map the report folder with ls, find and du, read permission strings, and fix a script that only ran in one folder on one computer

steps.text: Start the lab and see where you are: pwd, ls -a
Map the logs with find, ls -S and du
Read the permission strings of listing.txt and answer in answers.md
Fix run_counts.sh: its own folder, and quotes round a folder name with a space
Run it from the workspace folder and check the lab

lab.stretch: On a Linux workspace, make run_counts.sh executable with chmod u+x, run it as ./run_counts.sh, and explain why bash run_counts.sh never needed that

sessions.title: Pipes, redirection and filters
sessions.summary: Small programs joined by pipes answer counting questions over thousands of lines
outcomes: Chain head, grep, cut, sort, uniq and wc into a pipeline that answers one question
Redirect output and errors to files
Find a hidden character or a repeated line that skews a count

lab.title: A counting pipeline over synthetic logs
lab.summary: Six counts over twelve stations' October logs, one pipeline each, saved as counts.sh and checked against the reference values

steps.text: Look at the logs: head, tail, wc -l
Count the reading lines without comments or blank lines (Q1)
Lines per status, and the carriage-return trap (Q2)
The three stations with most errors, and each error code (Q3, Q4)
Duplicate lines after a restart, and stations per client from the CSV (Q5, Q6)
Save the output to counts.txt and check the lab

lab.stretch: Count the alert hours (PM10 above 150) per station with awk, each station and hour counted once

sessions.title: Environment variables, exit codes and remote login
sessions.summary: A script that takes its input from outside, says when it failed, and a key pair to log in elsewhere
outcomes: Pass a folder as an argument with an environment variable as the fallback
Make a script stop with a non-zero exit code and a message on stderr
Create an SSH key pair, read its fingerprint and write a host entry

lab.title: The counting script on a second folder, and a practice key
lab.summary: Addition to the entry's labs. Make the counting script run unchanged on November's logs, fail clearly, and create a practice SSH key pair and host entry for the lab workspace

steps.text: Take the folder as $1, with AIR_LOGS as the fallback
Stop with exit code 2 and a message on stderr; set -euo pipefail
Run it unchanged on the November folder
Make a practice Ed25519 key pair in keys/ and save its fingerprint
Write the ssh_config entry and check the lab

lab.stretch: Log in to the provided Linux workspace with the key (ssh -F ssh_config lab-workspace) and run counts.sh there on its copy of the logs

sessions.title: Commits, staging and history
sessions.summary: A commit is a snapshot with a parent; a branch is a name that points at one
outcomes: Draw the commit graph that a sequence of commands produces
Tell what is changed, what is staged and what is committed
Read git log --graph and match it to a drawing

lab.title: Draw the graph, then check it
lab.summary: Addition to the entry's labs. Predict the commit graph of three short command sequences on paper, run them in a practice repository, and compare with git log --graph

steps.text: Predict, then run sequence 1
Compare with git log --graph and correct your drawing
Sequence 2: stage one change of two and read both diffs
Sequence 3: a branch that moves while main moves too
Answer the four questions and check the lab

lab.stretch: Predict what git commit --amend does to the last circle of your drawing, then try it and compare the commit ids before and after

days.subtitle: Find, count and script in the shell, then draw what Git records

days.title: Working together on one history

sessions.title: Branches, merges and conflicts
sessions.summary: Two lines of work join in a merge; when both changed the same lines, a person decides
outcomes: Tell a fast-forward from a merge commit on a graph
Read conflict markers and keep both changes where both are right
Push, fetch and read origin/main as the hub's last known state

lab.title: Merge two branches and resolve a conflict alone
lab.summary: Addition to the entry's labs. Merge the analyst's and the technician's branches into main, resolve the conflict on the threshold line so both changes survive, and push to the hub

steps.text: Read the graph and both branches
Merge the first branch: a fast-forward
Merge the second and read the conflict markers
Resolve so both changes survive, and commit
Push to the hub, fetch, read origin/main and check the lab

lab.stretch: In a copy, put the second branch on top of main with git rebase instead, and compare the two graphs

sessions.title: Pull requests and review etiquette
sessions.summary: Main changes only through small, reviewed requests; a good comment names a line and a reason
outcomes: Open a small pull request from a branch with a title that says what changes
Write review comments that name a line and a reason, and answer them with commits
Resolve a conflict on your own branch before the merge

lab.title: Branch, review and resolve a conflict in teams of three
lab.summary: Two authors and a reviewer on a hub whose main is protected: two pull requests on the report rules, comments addressed, one conflict resolved on the branch, both merged

steps.text: Take roles; try to push to main and read the refusal
Authors: one branch, one commit and one pull request each
Reviewer: one comment per request with a line and a reason; authors answer with a commit
Merge the first; the second author merges main into the branch and resolves
Reviewer approves the new commits; merge and check the lab

lab.stretch: Write the team's five-line review checklist and add it through a third pull request

sessions.title: Undoing mistakes
sessions.summary: Each mistake has its own undo, and a pushed commit is undone with a new one
outcomes: Choose between restore, amend, reset and revert for a given mistake
Undo a pushed commit without rewriting what others pulled
Recover a lost commit or branch from the reflog

lab.title: Undo five mistakes
lab.summary: Addition to the entry's labs. A repository with five mistakes in it: a stray staged file and line, a local debug commit, a wrong message with a forgotten file, a pushed wrong threshold, a deleted branch

steps.text: Read the state: status, log and what is pushed
Unstage a file and discard a stray change with restore
Drop a local commit with reset and fix the last one with amend
Undo the pushed commit with revert, and push
Bring back the deleted branch from the reflog and check the lab

lab.stretch: For each of the five, write whether the same undo is safe after a push, and why

sessions.title: Virtual environments and lock files
sessions.summary: Declare what the project needs, lock the exact versions, and rebuild from the lock
outcomes: Explain why a project runs on one machine and fails on another
Declare dependencies and lock them with an environment manager
Rebuild a fresh environment from the lock and compare the output

lab.title: Rescue a project that fails on a second machine
lab.summary: Clone the analyst's report project as a second machine, read why it fails, then declare, pin and lock its dependencies and rebuild it to the expected output

steps.text: Clone to a second machine, run it and read each failure
Name the causes: an undeclared package, a path on one computer, no versions
Declare with uv init and uv add, pin Python, lock
Take the data folder as an argument; rebuild fresh and compare
Commit pyproject.toml and uv.lock; check the lab

lab.stretch: Do the same with pip-tools (requirements.in, pip-compile --generate-hashes) and compare the two lock files

days.subtitle: Branches, reviewed pull requests, conflicts, undoing, and an environment that rebuilds

days.title: Rebuild anywhere, leak nothing

sessions.title: One command to rebuild and run
sessions.summary: A reader rebuilds the result with one documented command, and the repository holds code, not data or outputs
outcomes: Keep data and outputs out of the repository and say where they come from
Write one documented command that rebuilds and checks the result
Test a README by following it in a clean clone

lab.title: One command, and data kept out of the code
lab.summary: Addition to the entry's labs. Stop tracking the data and output the report project carries, write rebuild.sh with an expected checksum and a Reproduce section, and follow it in a clean clone

steps.text: List what the repository carries with git ls-files
Stop tracking data and output: git rm --cached and .gitignore
Write rebuild.sh: sync the lock, run, compare with the expected checksum
Write the README's Reproduce section
Clone to a clean folder, follow the README only, and check the lab

lab.stretch: Make rebuild.sh print the versions it ran with (uv, Python, the locked packages) so a reproduction log can quote them

sessions.title: Images, containers and volumes
sessions.summary: An image is built once from a short definition; each run is a container that sees only what you mount
outcomes: Tell an image from a container and a layer from a mount
Write a short container definition that installs from the lock
Run a container without administrator rights with data mounted read-only

lab.title: Containerise the project with a mounted data folder, on a laptop or a provided Linux workspace
lab.summary: Complete a five-line container definition that installs from the lock, build it with a rootless engine, and run the report with the logs mounted read-only

steps.text: Check the engine runs without administrator rights
Export the lock as hashed requirements
Complete the five lines of the Containerfile
Build the image
Run it with the logs mounted read-only and the output mounted; compare and check

lab.stretch: Read the image's layers (podman image history), change report.py, and see which layers rebuild

sessions.title: What a container does not isolate, and keys in the environment
sessions.summary: A container shares the kernel, the mounts and every variable you pass it; a key belongs in the environment, never in the code
outcomes: Name what a container shares with its host
Read a key from the environment and stop clearly when it is missing
Keep the key out of the output and the repository, with an example file in its place

lab.title: The key out of the code
lab.summary: Addition to the entry's labs. Move the report-portal key from the code into an environment variable, with .env.example committed, .env ignored and the key masked in the output

steps.text: Find the key in the code and in the output of a run
Read it from AIR_PORTAL_KEY; stop with exit 2 when it is missing
Write .env.example, keep .env ignored, run with uv run --env-file
Print only the key's last four characters
Commit, find the key still in history with git log -S, and check the lab

lab.stretch: Run the container with --env-file .env and list what else the container can see: its variables and its mounts

sessions.title: Scanning before each commit, and after a leak
sessions.summary: Scan before every commit; after a leak, rotate first, then clean the history and report
outcomes: Run a secret scan over files, staged changes and the whole history
Carry out the leak response in order: rotate, clean, report
Install a commit hook that refuses a commit holding a key

lab.title: Remediate a seeded leaked key with a scanner and a commit hook
lab.summary: A key leaked in an old commit: find it with a scan of the history, revoke and replace it, write the rotation note, clean the history, and install a hook that blocks the next one

steps.text: Scan the whole history and find the key
Rotate first: revoke the old key and issue a new one into .env
Write ROTATION.md
Clean the history with git filter-repo, force-push, scan again
Install the hook, see it block a key, and check the lab

lab.stretch: Run gitleaks with the repository's .gitleaks.toml, or the class host's push protection, and compare what it finds with the course scanner

days.title: Capstone: peer reproduction
days.subtitle: A peer rebuilds your repository from its README on a clean workspace; then a short oral on one failed step

capstone.summary: A peer reproduces the participant's repository from the README on a clean workspace; the follow-up task fixes each failed step and records a second, successful reproduction
capstone.submission: Individual. A link to a public GitHub repository of the participant's own small project, on synthetic or public data only: a README with a Reproduce section, a lock file, a container definition, the secret-scan configuration and a clean scan of the whole history. On the capstone day a peer reproduces it on a clean workspace and files the reproduction log as a pull request; within the follow-up task the participant fixes every failed step and the peer records a second, successful reproduction. Then a seven-minute oral: three minutes on one failed step and its fix, four of questions.

rubric.criterion: README: prerequisites, where the data comes from, one documented rebuild command and the expected output
Clean rebuild: on the peer's clean workspace the locked environment rebuilds and reproduces the expected output
Container: the definition installs from the lock, runs without administrator rights and reads mounted data
Hygiene: configuration read from the environment, a clean scan of the whole history, no data or outputs committed
History: small commits merged through reviewed pull requests, with the peer's log merged by pull request
Follow-up: every step the peer could not follow fixed, and the second reproduction log successful
